executive_assessment.text: Three-commune evidence shows differing hazards and migration mediated by poverty, debt and employment, rather than direct hazard-triggered migration.
Tonle Sap's forced settlement illustrates how lost mobility and fishing access can increase exposure; WASH risks and local adaptation networks add capacity detail without causal outcome claims.

geographic_notes.text: In the July 2023 three-commune study, respondents described drought/floods in Kanhchor, heatwaves in Sre Ktum and windstorms in Kbal Romeas; these are reported local hazards, not measured hazard frequencies.
The study says weather-related crop and property losses reduce income; poverty, debt and job scarcity mediate work migration, while hazards were not direct triggers.
In 2023, Sre Ktum received over USD 70,000 through REDD+ across three community protected areas; WCS, WWF and the commune discussed livelihood-diversification uses.
The 2024 ethnographic article describes the 2018 forced relocation of three Tonle Sap floating communities in Kampong Chhnang—Chhnok Tru, Kampong Preah and Seh Slab—home to more than 4,000 people.
The Tonle Sap ethnography describes forced settlement preventing seasonal movement with floodwaters, narrowing fishing access and increasing flood/storm exposure and travel costs.
The authors describe altered flood pulses and fisheries decline amid dams, climate change, intensive agriculture and land development; individual drivers are not isolated.
Across eight Tonle Sap villages, 96% of sampled households reported drought; common responses were changing planting time (65%), while only 12% increased irrigation.
Perceived peer effects were positively associated with multiple adaptive practices, but not irrigation or fertilizer choices; authors cite resource-access and infrastructure constraints.
NGO and private-vendor ties moderated peer effects in the study models; government ties did not change the modeled relationship with adaptation intensity.

known_gaps.text: No inspected source explicitly links climate hazards to conflict or violence; no country-specific climate-FCV pathway is asserted.
NDC hazard and vulnerability estimates rely partly on cited secondary studies; underlying methods were not separately assessed.
NDC WASH commitments and targets are plans, not evidence of implementation or service outcomes.
Draft collection pending human source review and approval. IDA eligibility is not an FCV classification.
National and selected local examples do not establish district-level coverage or causal attribution.
The bank contains no completed mediated climate-FCV pathway; this is an evidence gap, not evidence of absence.
No current primary source in this batch substantiates climate-driven organized violence in Cambodia; migration and gendered safety risks are kept to their source-stated scope.
The Tonle Sap relocation study is qualitative and does not estimate population prevalence; the CDRI migration results are from three communes and households already containing migrants.
UNICEF/SIWI report publication corrected to August 2024 from its copyright and suggested citation; the raw intake's September 2023 date was not retained.
Forced relocation and lost mobility are documented historical vulnerabilities; neither migration nor gendered safety risk is recast as organized violence.
Draft extension: human source review and approval remain pending. Lending eligibility is not an FCV classification.
